title: NGC 6822 and its rich neighborhood
caption: The irregular galaxy NGC 6822, imaged by the Blanco 4-meter Telescope

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Countless hot, blue, massive stars and several well-known nebulae stand out in this color image of NGC 6822, a nearby irregular galaxy. Found in the constellation Sagittarius, approximately 1.6 million light-years from Earth, it is a member of the Local Group, the family of galaxies that includes the Milky Way.

E. E. Barnard discovered NGC 6822 in the early 1880s. Edwin P. Hubble made the first detailed study of it in 1925, with the then-new 100-inch telescope on Mount Wilson. In 1966 Susan E. Kayser, then a graduate student, analyzed those photographic plates, and her work remained the most complete study of the galaxy until these new observations.

An irregular galaxy has no clear spiral or elliptical form. The many blue massive stars in NGC 6822 are young, since such stars burn out quickly, which tells astronomers that NGC 6822 has formed stars recently.
scale: NGC 6822 lies approximately 1.6 million light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Blanco 4-meter telescope's Mosaic II camera observed NGC 6822 in eight filters. Travis Rector combined seven of them, with U shown as violet, B as blue, V as green, R as orange, I as red, hydrogen-alpha as red and oxygen (O III) as blue.

understand.eye: The U filter records near-ultraviolet light the eye barely sees, and narrow hydrogen and oxygen filters pick out glowing nebulae far too faint to see directly.

explore: The images were taken in eight filters with the Blanco 4-meter telescope at Cerro Tololo, near La Serena, Chile, by CTIO staff Knut Olsen and Chris Smith, part of the Local Group Galaxies Survey Team led by Phil Massey of Lowell Observatory. The survey was one of 13 active survey projects supported by the National Optical Astronomy Observatory.
